source.title: Putting a Face to Forgetting: Continual Learning meets Mechanistic Interpretability
source.authors: Sergi Masip Cabeza; Gido M. van de Ven; Javier Ferrando; T. Tuytelaars

record.tranche_reason: The study examines feature capacity and overlap in a sparse, overcomplete toy feature-reader model, but does not test how superposition is formed or measure its static packing geometry.
record.gate_note: The toy experiments impose a known feature basis and an overcomplete representation (80 features to 20 dimensions, with 90% activation sparsity), then report capacity and overlap dynamics during continual learning. They vary task overlap, contribution alignment, probe count, and depth—not activation sparsity itself. The ViT case study is not an LLM and does not test the listed LLM claims. Crosscoder caveats are stated, but their stability or completeness is not experimentally tested.
record.test_reason: The study takes superposition and allocated capacity (from Elhage et al. and Scherlis et al.) as its framework for explaining catastrophic forgetting. Its toy 'feature-reader' model fixes overcompleteness by design: 80 known features in 20 dimensions, with feature vectors optimized directly and a task probe instead of reconstruction. It then measures how capacity, overlap, fading and misalignment change across sequential tasks. It never tests whether superposition arises, what geometry it takes, whether there is a sparsity-dependent transition, or why neurons are polysemantic. Sparsity is fixed at 90%. The ViT crosscoder case study uses SAEs/crosscoders as a tracking tool and does not test their completeness, stability or canonicity. The rows measure a related but different construct (forgetting dynamics of an imposed superposed code), so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: forgetting is framed as feature-vector rotations and scalings that reduce allocated capacity (overlap, fading) or cause readout misalignment. The toy model confirms the best-case and worst-case predictions and shows that depth is harmful. The ViT crosscoder study is a preliminary demonstration, with fading dominating in the task-incremental setting and overlap mattering more in the class-incremental setting.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a feature-reader model with known feature activations and direct feature-vector optimization for continual-learning analysis, plus crosscoders for a ViT case study; it does not reproduce the original superposition-training method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported geometry and forgetting outcomes vary with task overlap, contribution alignment, number of probes, depth, and task-incremental versus class-incremental setup.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy model with imposed superposition (80 features in 20 dims), shared-but-misaligned task features cause capacity degradation (overlap and fading) and forgetting. Disjoint features are shielded, and more probes and greater depth amplify degradation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposed feature codes are vulnerable to capacity degradation under continual learning when features are coactive across tasks with differing contributions.

record.problems: The toy model assumes the feature identities are known and directly optimizes feature vectors. Superposition is imposed by the overcomplete setup rather than shown to emerge; activation sparsity is not varied. The practical demonstration is described by the authors as limited-scale and preliminary, and they say crosscoder sensitivity to variability remains untested. Results are often presented in plots without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported per-depth or per-probe numeric figure values were extracted; the text gives aggregate trends for these sweeps (Figures 3 and 4).

untested.parts: Emergence of superposition, near-orthogonal packing, sparsity-dependent phase transition, regular geometry (overcompleteness imposed; sparsity fixed at 90%).
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity; dedicated dimensions for important features.
No LLM studied; ViT SAE features used as a tool only.
Crosscoder stability/completeness explicitly flagged by the authors as untested.
Linear 1-D features assumed; multidimensional features only mentioned as a limitation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. The study cites the original superposition paper and builds on its capacity metric but does not test superposition itself. The ViT crosscoder results (Figs. 7–9, 11) are not recorded as rows; that is appropriate, since they bear on forgetting, not on V4 or V5.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures capacity and overlap changes in an already overcomplete toy representation, but does not test formation of superposition, near-orthogonal packing, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular static geometry.
It does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important ones share.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
The practical case study is a Vision Transformer, not an LLM; it does not test feature spread across LLM neurons or SAE recovery of LLM features.
The study cautions that crosscoder features are approximate and potentially sensitive to modeling choices, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The study assumes linear feature directions and mentions multidimensional features as a limitation, but does not test feature dimensionality.

rows.subject: feature-reader model
rows.operation_detail: Measured change in feature overlap and fading during sequential task learning.

conditions.value: Full: features coactive across tasks; task-specific features have nonzero contribution

rows.value: The Full scenario produces more capacity degradation through increasing overlap and fading than the None scenario.
rows.uncertainty: Average of 5 independent seeds; no error bar or interval stated.
rows.note: This tracks geometry changes in a representation where overcompleteness is imposed; it does not establish the initial feature packing.
rows.check: Measures change in overlap/fading during continual learning in an imposed overcomplete code (Full vs None, Fig. 2). This is not whether or how superposition forms, nor its geometry. Not a V1 test.

rows.subject: feature-reader model
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature-capacity changes in the disjoint-feature scenario.

conditions.value: None: tasks use disjoint feature sets

rows.baseline: Full scenario: features coactive across tasks
rows.value: The disjoint-feature scenario has low capacity degradation; the text also reports that depth has a milder but still present effect in this scenario.
rows.uncertainty: Average of 5 independent seeds; no error bar or interval stated.
rows.note: The disjoint condition is described as shielding old features from task-training gradients in the single-layer analysis.
rows.check: Control condition for the forgetting comparison (disjoint features). Bears on forgetting dynamics, not on any superposition version.

rows.subject: feature-reader model
rows.operation_detail: Measured capacity degradation while varying the number of probes reading the activation.
rows.value: Increasing the number of probes amplifies capacity degradation and forgetting.
rows.uncertainty: Average of 5 independent seeds; no error bar or interval stated.
rows.note: This concerns geometry changes under continual-learning updates, not a sparsity sweep or initial superposition geometry.
rows.check: Probe-count sweep affects capacity degradation under continual learning. Unrelated to V1's sparsity transition or packing geometry.

rows.subject: feature-reader model
rows.operation_detail: Measured allocated-capacity metrics across encoder depth.
rows.value: Depth causes severe capacity degradation in Full; the effect is milder but still present in None.
rows.uncertainty: Average of 5 independent seeds; no error bar or interval stated.
rows.note: The text describes the trend across the depth sweep; it does not give per-depth numeric values.
rows.check: Depth sweep of capacity degradation in a deep linear encoder (Fig. 3). A forgetting result, not a superposition test.

rows.subject: feature-reader model
rows.operation_detail: Varied feature overlap and contribution alignment across tasks and measured capacity dynamics.
rows.value: At full overlap and perfect contribution alignment, the text says feature geometry is almost entirely preserved; at full overlap and extreme conflicting alignment, the text reports geometric rearrangement despite increased feature capacity and norms.
rows.uncertainty: Average of 5 independent seeds; no error bar or interval stated.
rows.note: This tests how task contribution and coactivation conditions affect geometry in an imposed overcomplete representation; no activation-sparsity sweep is reported.
rows.check: Task overlap × contribution alignment grid (Fig. 10, App. E.1). It reports forgetting values (e.g. 0.36, 0.33, 0.21) and geometric rearrangement under conflict. Still forgetting dynamics, not superposition formation or geometry. Baseline is the zero-overlap column, not 'not stated'.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Feature-reader toy model; varied task overlap and contribution alignment
reader_labels.reason: The reported capacity and overlap dynamics vary with task coactivation and contribution conditions in an overcomplete sparse representation (R1, R5). This supports only that limited geometric aspect, not the claimed packing geometry or sparsity transition.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature-reader toy model; disjoint tasks, probe-count sweep, and depth sweep
reader_labels.reason: Capacity outcomes also depend on task structure, number of probes, and depth; the study does not establish the proposed static geometry or its dependence on activation sparsity (R2, R3, R4).
